title: The Computer Science Theorems Database — Theorems 1–3

Statement: No algorithm can decide, for every program-input pair, whether the program halts. Why it matters: it constrains what is possible and guides every correct design in its domain. Theorem 2: Cook–Levin Theorem. Statement: Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete: every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. Why it matters: it constrains what is possible and guides every correct design in its domain. Worked example: see the verified demo, which computes a concrete instance.

Theorem 3: Church–Turing Thesis. Statement: Any function effectively calculable by a human following rules is computable by a Turing machine. Why it matters: it constrains what is possible and guides every correct design in its domain. Worked example: see the verified demo, which computes a concrete instance.

title: The Computer Science Theorems Database — Theorems 4–6

Theorem 5: Master Theorem. Statement: Recurrences T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) solve to Θ(n^(log_b a)), Θ(n^(log_b a) log n), or Θ(f(n)) by case. Why it matters: it constrains what is possible and guides every correct design in its domain. Worked example: see the verified demo, which computes a concrete instance.

Theorem 12: Central Limit Theorem. Statement: Sums of independent, finite-variance variables converge to a normal distribution. Why it matters: it constrains what is possible and guides every correct design in its domain. Worked example: see the verified demo, which computes a concrete instance.

body:

Worked example: see the verified demo, which computes a concrete instance.
